about: The phrase “Cálicem salutáris” comes from Psalm 115:4: “I will take the chalice of salvation, and call upon the name of the Lord.” The closing petition returns to the biblical “odor suavitátis”, a description of an offering made to the Lord (for example, Lev 1:9). The verb “ascéndat” asks that the chalice ascend before God.

s01.narrative: The priest takes the chalice, wine and water now mixed in it, and raises it.

s02.translation: We offer Thee, Lord, the chalice of salvation, beseeching Thy clemency: that it may go up with a sweet fragrance in the sight of Thy divine majesty, for our salvation and that of the whole world. Amen.

w001.function: Plural: at solemn Mass the deacon says this prayer with the priest — unlike over the host, where it was “óffero”. At low Mass the priest says it alone, for all.

w005.function: The genitive of the noun salutáre (salvation), not the adjective: an adjective would have to agree with “cálicem” (w004), which stands in the accusative. The same phrase returns in the priest's verses before Communion.

w006.function: Agrees with “cleméntiam” (w008), two words away — Latin parts such pairs freely.

w007.function: The participle refers to the unwritten subject of “Offérimus” (w001): we offer — beseeching.

w008.function: Deprecor takes an accusative: to entreat someone, or for something.

w016.function: Agrees with “salúte” (w020), four words away. The form would also allow a neuter plural, but the agreement settles it.

w020.function: One “salvation” for two modifiers: ours and the whole world's.

w023.function: A genitive where a modern tongue would put an adjective — a Hebrew turn kept in Latin: fragrance of sweetness for “sweet fragrance”.

w024.function: Its subject is the chalice. Subjunctive after “ut” (w009).
